The mechanics in this game make for an interesting time. Snooping through someone's phone for clues about the disappearance of a girl is very satisfying and the characters and plot make for a well paced and entertaining few hours. 

That being said I don't think there was much optimization done for PC. You're better off playing this on mobile as originally intended.

You find a young woman's phone and find out she is a missing person. You use clues within the phone to solve what happened to her. You interract with her friends and her 'dates'. You impact their lives with what you tell them or do to them. I literally laughed out loud at some of the things I said or did to the characters. I really enjoyed the mystery and problem solving up until the end. You have I think 3 endings and none of them are truly satisfying. The villain and ending isn't really satisfying. It's kind of a chessy B-Movie. You enjoy the characters but overall it's let down a bit by the end. It's original though and I will be playing it's sequel, even though I'm not sure how a sequel will work given the ending.

It's an ok idea ruined by bad not the greatest acting and thottery.
Levels designed with Simps in mind such as unlock a selfie of her in gym gear.
It's not worth the hassle when thottery is so strong, and I'm no simp, therefore there's little appeal to me.
If you're gonna made a scary mystery puzzle game, don't just push the story half way...
You gotta step it up and make it scary, images need to be messed up, the psychological part needs make the player feel uneasy.

To conclude:

This is a puzzle game where you unlock selfies of a girl who knows shes attractive, which gets boring pretty fast.

The plot of this game is basically: 
you find a phone. The owner is apparently missing, and you check her phone in order to find her and what happened to her.

The idea sounds interesting on the paper. In reality, it's not well executed. Game isn't really good. 
1. The people you interact with. They are supposed to be in their 20's/30's... but they behave like 10 years old (especially Taylor and Greg... ). Most of the jokes are kinda lame too.
2. The acting is not that good either. 
3. The only decent thing in this game is maybe the "scary" elements, which don't happen often. 
Sometimes you can hear a voice whispering in your ear, I guess this is used to create some scare jump situation. This could be an interesting feature, however your character doesn't react at all to it. So... there is hardly any point to it. It's kinda out of place 

I heard that the second game is much better...

if you want some good games in which you interact with people using a phone/chat, you should instead try the game serie "Emilie Is Away" (the first game is free on Steam).
Holy crap! Talk about keeping you on the edge of your seat! This game is something special and no words or reviews can do it any Justice.. Just play it!!
The game is kind of fun. The premise is kind of interesting. It's not a bad game, but the writing is poor and the voice acting is amazingly cheesy.

I don't review a lot, but I had to speak up on this one. This game is a tough one to rate though, because it did pull me in with the interesting UI and the depth of stuff you could look at, but after about an hour I started suspecting that this game was kind of dumb, and now I know for sure that I think it is The characters are unlikable, they don't act like real people, and the dialogue is mostly pretty bad and poorly translated. It's also really annoying when the characters text ONE WORD, and you're watching as 17 text messages fly by, wondering if the train of thought will ever end! Not to mention that the acting is very amateurish. The highest compliment I can give this game is that Anna is really hot, but she's also a pretty bad actress, so.....

It kept my attention and refreshing to see a different style of game. It has a chilled vibe, though 'Horror' may be a bit of a stretch. 
It is a short game however for the low price that's kind of expected. 
The end for me was a bit meh, I'd made up these elaborate assumptions  of how it was going to unravel so was a little let down.  There was a lot left unknown which I was sad never got answered.  It's fun figuring things out. I enjoyed, will play number 2.

Creepy af. Very intuitive UI. Engaging storyline. Very immersive with headphones on and the lights off. Probably not the scariest thing you've ever played, but it's plenty suspenseful and even has a few jumpscare moments. Very cool the way they made it so that you play the entire game looking at the virtual screen of this virtual phone you discovered mysteriously. That's it, that's all the gameplay is, sending "texts", reading "emails", watching "videos"...all while trying to determine literally everything about this person who the phone belongs to, as well as determining what exactly is going on with the mysterious antagonist of the game. All in all, well worth the price, and the time spent playing. I made it thru one full playthru in 7 hours, but at least 2-3 of those hours was me walking away for awhile and coming back fresh.

[h1]Short but Intuitive Mystery Game[/h1]

[i]SIMULACRA[/i] is a modern FMV game that features great sleuthing gameplay with some minor horror elements. After I 100% the entire game, I can safely say this is one of the better indie visual novel titles I've encountered if not for the gameplay alone. I will try to keep this review mostly spoiler-free, but as usual with my reviews for narrative-based games, I will have spoilers for stuff I feel the need to comment on. 

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The gameplay and puzzles are fun yet intuitive. I like the process of fixing corrupted messages and images to not only progress the game but to also discover more about the characters.
[*] Lots of "show don't tell" moments that exemplify how the developers understand that this is a visual medium and that it is important to use the visuals to their advantage. For example, though it's never stated Anna is into fitness, one of the first image puzzles is of her posing with weights to give the idea that she is an active person. This is great  yet subtle storytelling I love to see in these types of games. 
[*] The text messages and dating profiles are pretty genuine. There are definitely people out there who act exactly like the ones in this game.
[*] The narrative does a lot to try and make you question the motives of the characters and their backgrounds in a meaningful way so that the suspense is maintained the entire playthrough. 
[*] [spoiler] The main antagonist being a serial killer HAL-9000-esque AI in the phone itself is fascinating in its own right, and the fact that its goal is to create perfect versions of otherwise "pathetic worms" as it refers to people it deems as as such, is great social commentary on how people are obsessed with their public image online to the point that they are no longer genuinely themselves. The antagonist also serves as a personification of tech companies and their obsession to mold people into their idealized image through deceptive practices and establishing trust by packaging things in digestible ways. For example, during the phone reset, the soothing sounds and use of cool hues is meant to contrast with the otherwise invasive questions and disturbing content the OS system tries to get you to answer in detail. In the end, you get the best ending by impressing the AI with your ability to manipulate the characters--an interesting moral dilemma to say the least!  [/spoiler]
[*] The menus and apps look and feel like their real version counterparts. Very good overall graphical presentation. 
[*] Small and subtle changes to show you are progressing through the story. For example, [spoiler] Anna's picture in the home screen will change expression the closer you get to the ending of the game. [/spoiler]
[*] Lots of small things to discover just by exploring the phone (which you can get achievements for). 
[*] Sped up dialog loading for additional playthroughs is a great QoL feature. 
[/olist]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The voice acting and FMV sequences come across as cheesy most of the time, if not overacted. 
[*] The autosave feature means you can't go back to a previous part like you can with most visual novels. This means that if you messed up on a certain decision, you may have to restart the entire run just to redo it. This can be pretty frustrating. 
[*] No option to skip puzzles for additional playthroughs means you'll have to do them over and over again which can be pretty tedious if you're trying to get all the achievements. 
[*] The dialogue choices you  need to appease and have Taylor trust you come across as a bit too flirty at times.
[*] Greg and Ashley come across as too angry and distrustful to the player character depending on certain choices made. Meanwhile, Taylor comes across as too trusting. This is why sometimes it's not very good to have a faceless protagonist--we don't really understand what the characters see in [i]you[/i] when the interactions are so minimal. 
[*] The horror elements are too on the nose with the jumpscares. Though the phone OS does have some good subtle horror elements, more of this throughout the game would have been way better overall. 
[*] [spoiler] Though I like the idea of the antagonist, having it type in predictable shaky font and using distorted visuals is pretty cliche. Personally, I think it'd come across scarier if it were way more subtle like how it is when the phone resets.[/spoiler]
[/olist]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Worth at least one playthrough--though playing it blind is your best bet. The gameplay alone makes it worth it. For additional playthroughs, some patience is required. Watch additional endings via recordings if that's not your thing.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
You found a lost phone. Inside, you find someone asking for help. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] puts you in the shoe of a stranger who is trying to find the owner of a lost phone. Will you succeed or will you fail?

[b]Pros:[/b]

- New game plus let you play the game with faster chat speed

[b]Cons:[/b]

- Not suitable for people who have issues with flashing lights

[b]Specs[/b]
Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read a visual novel that was told through phone and chats, feel free to buy this game at a sale.[/i]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
As a game that is played out on a smartphone, the game does well to simulate the phone-like interface. It has a photo app, a contact book, a chat app - anything that you'll expect from a smartphone. Its functionality is limited tough. There is no option to switch between tabs nor a scroll bar on the right side of the screen to scroll the page faster.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is played out from series of chats. Expect a lot of typos and shortened words due to the informal context. This brings forth the characters' personality though, especially since everyone has a unique texting style from each other. Some information can also be retrieved by watching videos and receiving phone calls, although their voice is not expressive enough - it feels dragged out on purpose to make it easier for non-native English speakers to listen to. It does make them easier to hear, but it also kills their expression in the process.

Interface aside, the presentation helps with the storytelling. The glitchy screen and a few jumpscares help to set the mysterious vibe, while the surprising phone calls freak me out sometimes. It got toned down as you play the game, focusing more on the mysterious element. The writing was done well in regards to what's happening and sometimes, you will have several options to choose from. Despite giving the same outcome, the conversation will play out differently based on which option that you choose. However, some sentences are not flowing smoothly after choosing a certain option, giving you the impression that you chose the wrong one.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225479 

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay is focused on chatting with people and exploring everything that is inside the phone that you used. As I said before, sometimes you will have to choose between several options to proceed. Some of them will affect the endings, some are not. Some old chat and photos will also be encrypted, allowing you to play a minigame to restore their state, which takes form in arranging photos or word. It's quite easy to finish although some words might be difficult to arrange sometimes.

Hints are usually provided whenever you are stuck. You can ask people to figure out what you are supposed to do and they will gladly help you out. However, I got stuck twice with no idea to proceed. Although one is expected since I never do well with puzzles that have vague rules, another feels like they don't give enough hints to solve.

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
I finished the game in ~4h, and proceed to replay the game several times to get all achievements. The new game+ helps a lot by providing a faster chat speed, allowing you to finish the game faster. However, you still need to wait for the voice-over near the ending to finish, and they talk very slowly. It was tiring to wait for them to finish talking and playing the game several times to unlock all four endings become not fun anymore. I wish there is an option to fast-forward the game at this point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225684 

[b]Problems[/b]
Although the game has a phone-like interface, some quality of life features are missing, notably the option to switch tabs in the browser (or the option to keep existing tab), and the feature to start a video from a certain timestamp. There were also some occasions when I had to type some forms and I couldn't use the tab button in my keyboard to switch between text boxes. Lastly, there are some flashing lights near the ending - people who have issues with it might want to stay out of the game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
For a visual novel game, it still can be enjoyed with people who don't like to read a wall of text. You might need to read a lot, but they are mostly in the form of short chats which shouldn't take long to finish. The story picks up an interesting topic that is enhanced with its mysterious vibe, and although the story feels weak at times, it still proves to be an enjoyable read.

An unsettling narrative that employs our intuitive knowledge of phones as a framework for oddly intuitive deductions and uncanny subversions.

It’s not a wholly unique concept for horror, but plenty of what’s done through interaction distinguishes Simulacra from the other cursed-PC or texting-based games with an opinion about digital privacy. Even if my thoughts were first drawn to comparisons, the strength of that initial ambiguity set within the benign familiarity of a mobile OS had me playing along in no time.

While the fixation on relationship drama does drive the story, it also seems to conflict with Simulacra's insidious tone. Although, the seemingly necessary overindulgence in others’ personal affairs does heighten a different sense of uneasiness. When the pixels aren't going "boo", Simulacra can be immensely unnerving. Silent realizations even provoked chills on more than one occasion.

Even if the narrative isn't unexpectedly divergent, the amount of time I spent mulling over the game's events speaks to the impact that they had on my participation. There's a lot to unwrap here and no better way to learn more than to play it for yourself.

A story about an idiot surrounded by other idiots who sound like idiots.

At no point was there any reason to sympathize with Anna and her lifetime of bad decisions that got her into this mess. She's like the stereotypical white person in a horror movie whose phone suddenly goes to static and runs out of gas in the middle of the night in front of an obviously haunted house and says "I should investigate this immediately, and by myself!". Her dumbass ex, her dumbass new lover, her dumbass "best friend", all of whom supposedly want to help her yet they somehow form the main obstacles to doing so, especially the "best friend" who is basically a secondary antagonist for all the help she is. Aside from bit players like the completely unconvincing cop. I thought the cop was lying about being a cop and that that was important as first, but nope, just terrible voice acting, we're supposed to believe that's what cops sound like. Though he's not as bad as the villain revealed at the end, who sounds like a 13 year old boy who got his big brother to install voice changing software for him because he thinks it'll make him sound badass on voice chat while playing Halo. It's that bad. Was it supposed to be intimidating? Was it supposed to be a shocking reveal? It wasn't, just the annoying end to a nonsensical story about thoroughly unsympathetic idiots. Nothing about this is redeemable, this was a waste of a Humble Bundle pick. And they had the nerve to release a sequel? Why, because they can churn out terrible games like this once a week? I hope it at least has an "everyone dies" ending, because after meeting all of these characters, I honestly don't want any of them to live, it would be better for society for every one of them to go away.

A short supernatural investigative game that involves interacting with a cell phone which was left for you to find. You are given the task of finding out what happened to a girl named Anna whose phone you are now in possesion of. You investigate by interacting with individuals in her social media, dating app, email, phone contacts, and other media. Mostly you will choose from a pre-defined list of responses and actions, but there is some free play at times. 

There is a small puzzle element in that you need to "decrypt" her scrambled photos and text messages but it's fairly minor and doesn't really add anything to the experience. 

I have no idea if this was a mobile game first, but it does seem pretty ideal to be a mobile title. It still plays well on PC, but you'll be staring at the image of a phone 95% of the time. I use a dual monitor setup with my left monitor in portrait and my right in landscape so this was ideal to play on the portrait monitor while multitasking.

Simulacra is essentially a found footage film but as a game.
One day someone leaves you a phone at your doorstep, which belongs to a girl that has gone missing.
From there, it's your job to snoop through her phone to uncover hints on what happened to her.
The actors can be very cheesy and hardly believable, but that has it's own charm if you are into that kind of thing. The problem I had with the story was the horror elements that they try to shove in, in the form of jump scares. Apart from being the annoying type of jump scares, they also immediately take the story in a direction, where you as the player know where the story will end up. If the jump scares where replaced with more subtle hints that something is off, I think it would have been a lot more engaging.
  
To give credit to the devs, they did a good job at imitating a phone OS with  multiple apps. That makes it fun to snoop around for clues on how to gain access to specific parts of the phone. Even though you have a variety of apps to explore, however, multitasking is something that the fake OS lacks, which makes jumping back and forth from different apps a chore. Having to constantly scroll through everything to get to the part you need can quickly become a nuisance, especially when it deletes the things you have to fill in.

Despite these issues, I still enjoyed the game enough to recommend it for the price. It only takes around 3 to 4 hours to finish, but it has multiple endings. A new game plus mode exists, which fast-forwards the conversations. I wish it would skip the puzzles as well, so you can just focus on the endings, but alas, it is what it is.
Effective suspense thanks to the performances, writing and pacing. Definitely got goosebumps from a few of the atmospheric scares as well as the jump scares.

After an playing an hour of Simulacra and Simulacra 2 to review for the Humble Choice April 2021 Bundle:

These are a pair of horror or thriller games.  The first game spooked me with a major opening that has a lot of horror elements in it, but then didn’t do much with the horror aspect in the next 40 minutes.  Instead, it focused more on what life would be like as a woman.

Simulacra has you find a woman’s phone and then try to figure out what happened to her.  Though while playing it I noticed how freaking awful it would be to be a woman.  There’s a solid social commentary on how some people spoke to the mystery girl online and it’s done in a very strong way.  This isn’t social commentary being forced in there, but instead a strong point the game makes. 

The gameplay is mostly about snooping on the phone and has voyeuristic qualities to it.  You can even impersonate her with different people, and it’s quite interesting.  As much as I dislike the horror aspect in the beginning because I’m a scaredy-cat, I found myself wanting to play more as it’s more of a thriller.

Simulacra 2 seems to up the production values but presents a very similar experience.  Though I do want to mention there are a few grammar issues that I noticed in both games, and apparently, the team who created the game is from Malaysia, which might explain that.  Nothing that bad, but it can be a bit noticeable. 

Pick this up if you like horror or thriller, these aren’t long games, but they are unique.  There are some effective and interesting moments, such as hearing a woman’s voice from behind you if you’re playing wearing headphones.

Simulacra is an interactive horror movie displayed through an emulated mobile phone screen.  You've got someone else's phone and for some reason you're texting her boyfriend and watching spooky videos because something went wrong.  Spooky technology glitches! oooOOOoooo. 

I think FMV can be an excellent tool in storytelling and video game creation if used right.  Looking at games that worked, like Press X Not To Die and Mortal Kombat, you can see why.  Simulacra isn't one of the ones that works.  The story is below Blair Witch 4 kind of stuff, it's not gripping.  The bits where you're texting other people is badly written.  I understand the developers wanted to emulate a mobile phone, but looking at my 4K monitor being wasted displaying a 9:16 aspect ratio is just depressing.

There's better ways to tell a story than we can see in Simulacra.  For less money than they're asking for this you could rent any schlock horror film online and have a far better time, with better writing and acting, too.  If you did end up with this in the Humble Bundle and accidentally launched it, be aware the game crashes when you try to exit, and you have to go find the rogue process and kill it.

Got this via Humble ... but I gotta say, ugh, phff, well, no.

Maybe someone can find this interesting, but to me I just played it out of curiosity to see what it's about. And it only took 3 hours for 1 playthrough.

Gameplay is minimal. You "chat" with people mostly and sometimes you gotta play a bit of detective, but, nah.

I guess it might have been more interesting if the story had actually been good, if the characters had been likeable, but they're all very annoying people, even Ashley. Seriously, this game does not have a single human being ... or maybe it IS close to real and that would be even more depressing.

Using the apps was tedious, switching between apps meant progress was mostly lost, which slows down progress. Some hints are so "obscure" that you will have forgotten all about them when you actually need them halfway through the game. Some things are illogical.

The dialogue could carry such a game, but it's not well-written (and they do not speak EN as their mother tongue). It's cringy, annoying, irritating, endless (seriously, just write out the text in 1 message, not 10).

In any case the story makes little sense. Spoiler: It's not a thriller, it's "supernatural". That is made clear from the very beginning, but not on the store page. I expected an actual crime, not some pseudo horror trip with bad "explanations".

Honestly, I just wanted to tell the guys to leave me the fuck alone. I'll try out the 2nd game as well to see what they changed, but I do hope there's a "fuck you all" button.
